# Visual Statistical Analysis with ggstatsplot

[ggstatsplot](https://www.indrapatil.com/ggstatsplot/index.html) is an extension of ggplot package for creating graphics with defauls from statistical tests included in the information-rich plots themselves.

# Getting Started

## Installing of required packages

ggstatsplot and tidyverse is enough for this exercise.

```{r}
pacman::p_load(ggstatsplot, tidyverse)
```

## Importing data

For this exercise, Exam_data.csv is used.

```{r}
exam <- read_csv("data/Exam_data.csv")
```

# One-sample Test: gghistostats() method

The code chunk below will create a visual of one-sample test on English scores using [gghistostats()](https://www.indrapatil.com/ggstatsplot/reference/gghistostats.html).

```{r}
set.seed(1234)

gghistostats(
  data = exam,
  x = ENGLISH,
  type = "bayes",
  test.value = 60,
  xlab = "English scores"
)
```

## Unpacking the Bayes Factor

A Bayes factor is the ratio of the likelihood of one particular hypothesis to the likelihood of another. It can be interpreted as a measure of the strength of evidence in favor of one theory among two competing theories.

That's because the Bayes factor gives us a way to evaluate the data in facor of a null hypothesis, and to use external information to do so. It tells us what the weight of the evidence is in favor of a given hypothesis.

When we are comparing two hypotheses, H1 (the alternative hypothesis) and H0 (the null hypothesis), the Bayes Factor is often written as B10. It can be defined mathematically as

![](image1.jpg)

The Schwarz criterion is one of the easiest ways to calculate rough approximation of the Bayes factor.

## How to interpret Bayes Factor

A Bayes Factor can be any positive number. One of the most ocmmon interpretations is one firstly proposed by Harold Jeffereys (1961) and slightly modeified by Lee and Wagenmakers in 2013:

# Two-sample Mean Test: ggbetweenstats() method

The code chunk below, [ggbetweenstats()](https://www.indrapatil.com/ggstatsplot/reference/ggbetweenstats.html) is used to build a visual for two-sample mean test of Maths scores by gender.

```{r}
ggbetweenstats(data = exam,
               x = GENDER, 
               y = MATHS,
               type = "np",
               messages = FALSE)
```

# Oneway ANOVA Test: ggbetweenstats() method

`ggbetweenstats()` can be used to build a visual for one-way ANOVA test as shown in the code chunk below.

```{r}
ggbetweenstats(data = exam,
               x = RACE, 
               y = ENGLISH,
               type = "p",
               mean.ci = TRUE, 
               pairwise.comparisons = TRUE, 
               pairwise.display = "s",
               p.adjust.method = "fdr",
               messages = FALSE)
```

::: callout-note
Argument for `pairwise.display`:

-   "ns" --\> only non-significant
-   "s" --\> only significant 
-   "all" --\> everything
:::

# Significant Test of Correlation: ggscatterstats() method

In the code chunk below, [ggscaterstats()](https://www.indrapatil.com/ggstatsplot/reference/ggscatterstats.html) is used to build a visual for significant test of correlation between Maths score and English scores.

```{r}
ggscatterstats(data = exam,
               x = MATHS,
               y = ENGLISH,
               marginal = FALSE)
```

# Signidicant Test of Association (Dependence): ggbarstats() method

First, the Maths scores is binned into a 4-class variable using [cut()](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/base/versions/3.6.2/topics/cut).

```{r}
exam1 <- exam %>% 
  mutate(MATHS_bins = 
           cut(MATHS, 
               breaks = c(0,60,75,85,100)))
```

Then using that, we can use [ggbarstats()](https://www.indrapatil.com/ggstatsplot/reference/ggbarstats.html) to build a visual for significant test of association.

```{r}
ggbarstats(exam1, 
           x = MATHS_bins, 
           y = GENDER)
```
